text: Then came the strangest Sultan of all, Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
Clever, well-read and full of big ideas.
In 1327, he decided to move the capital from Delhi to Dalatabad, about a thousand kilometers south,
and he ordered much of Delhi's population to move with him.
Cheerful! Great news! We are moving the capital! Everybody back!
everybody your majesty everybody reading the map it's 40 days walk then start
walking a few years later he also issued copper and brass coins and declared them
worth the same as silver within months people were making their own coins at
at home, huge piles of fake money. He had to buy them all back with real silver. Shaking
his head, great idea, 500 years too early. In 1398, the Central Asian conqueror Timur
sacked Delhi. The city took a century to recover. Shatter. Meanwhile, in the south, a powerful
Hindu empire was rising, Vijayanagara, with its capital at Hampi. Foreign visitors said
it was as big as a room and full of diamonds and horses. But here was the thing about the
Sultanate years. Something new was also being made.
Bosun and Indian builders mixed their styles in arches, domes and minarets. The poet Amir
Khusrau wrote in a mix of Bosun and the local speech and is traditionally credited with
shaping kawali music. Out of the bazaars and army camps, a whole new language grew, what
would become Urdu and close cousin to Hindi. Absorb again. India doesn't just get invaded,
it gets remixed. In 1526, a young prince from Central Asia rode down from Kabul. He had
looking for a new one. His great great great grandfather was Timur and on his
mother's side he was descended from Genghis Khan.
